---
title: The truth manifest
guide-section: "Generating studies"
---

Real studies don't come with an answer key. Synthetic ones can: `Study.truth` records what a study
was built to show and what its generated data actually shows, so you can check an analysis program
against known values.

The manifest is a plain dictionary of JSON-compatible values, built after the study has passed its
checks. It holds two kinds of number:

- **Targets**: what the controls asked for, such as a mean change from baseline in each arm, a
median survival or a hazard ratio. These are properties of the population the study samples from.
- **Realized values**: what this study's datasets show, computed from its ADaM (or SDTM) the way a
standard analysis would compute them.

The two differ by sampling error, as a real study's estimates differ from the true effect.

## Targets and realized values

For a parallel-group study, the manifest has the target mean change from baseline in each arm, and
the mean change the study's ADaM realized at the end of treatment:

```{python}
import polars as pl
import trialforge as tf

trial = tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=300, seed=1, indication="hypertension", weeks=12)
trial.truth["endpoint"]
```

`paramcd` names the endpoint's parameter, and `visit` the analysis visit the realized values come
from. `n` in each arm is the number of subjects with a value at that visit, so it is smaller than the
number randomized when subjects discontinue.

## Reproducing a realized value

The realized values are computed from the generated ADaM datasets, so an analysis that reproduces
them reads the data correctly. Here the endpoint is systolic blood pressure in ADVS, and the end of
treatment is the week 12 analysis visit. Take the analysis records (`ANL01FL == "Y"`) at that visit,
then average the change from baseline by planned treatment:

```{python}
endpoint = trial.truth["endpoint"]

means = (
    trial.adam["ADVS"]
    .filter(
        pl.col("PARAMCD") == endpoint["paramcd"],
        pl.col("AVISIT") == "WEEK 12",
        pl.col("ANL01FL") == "Y",
        pl.col("CHG").is_not_null(),
    )
    .group_by("TRTP", maintain_order=True)
    .agg(n=pl.len(), mean_change=pl.col("CHG").mean().round(4))
)
means
```

The counts and means match `realized`, and their difference (Drug A minus placebo) is
`realized_difference`:

```{python}
mean = dict(zip(means["TRTP"], means["mean_change"]))
round(mean["Drug A 10 mg"] - mean["Placebo"], 4), endpoint["realized_difference"]
```

If your program gets a different answer from the same data, the manifest tells you where to look:
a different visit, missing the `ANL01FL` filter (which would count a subject twice when two of their
records fall in the visit's window), or the actual rather than the planned treatment.

## Sampling variation

The realized difference here is -7.2 mmHg against a target of -8. That is sampling error, not a
bias: the same request with other seeds gives other studies from the same population, scattered
around the target.

```{python}
[
    tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=300, seed=s, indication="hypertension", weeks=12)
    .truth["endpoint"]["realized_difference"]
    for s in range(1, 9)
]
```

This is what makes trialforge useful for simulation: generate many studies from one design, analyze
each one, and the spread of the estimates is the study's sampling distribution.

## What every manifest records

Every manifest records the request itself, so a manifest on its own says how to regenerate the
study:

```{python}
list(trial.truth)
```

`archetype`, `studyid`, `n` and `seed` are the arguments, `controls` the full set of controls the
study used (defaults included), and `arms` the arms in order. The rest depends on the archetype.

## Sections by archetype

| Archetype | Sections | What they report |
|---|---|---|
| `parallel_continuous` | `endpoint`, `discontinuation`, `teae_incidence`, and `non_inferiority` with `ni_margin` | Mean change at the end of treatment by arm; discontinuation by arm; subjects with a treatment-emergent AE |
| `dose_ranging_ph2` | as `parallel_continuous`, plus `dose_response` | Mean change per dose and the refitted Emax model (E0, Emax, ED50) against the target ED50 and Hill coefficient |
| `cns_alzheimers` | `adas_cog` | Baseline mean and change in the ADAS-Cog total by arm, both observed and with LOCF |
| `cv_outcomes` | `outcomes` | Events, Kaplan-Meier medians and a stratified Cox hazard ratio for MACE, each component and all-cause death; first MACE events against the target |
| `oncology_solid_tumor` | `targets`, `overall_survival`, `progression_free_survival`, `confirmed_orr`, `calibration` | Kaplan-Meier medians and stratified Cox hazard ratios; confirmed RECIST response rates |
| `heme_lymphoma` | as `oncology_solid_tumor`, with `orr` | The same, with Lugano 2014 response rates |
| `phase1_sad_mad` | `pk` | The population PK model; geometric means of the NCA parameters by dose; the power-model slope for dose proportionality |
| `crossover_be` | `bioequivalence` | For AUC and Cmax: the geometric mean ratio, its 90% confidence interval, the intra-subject CV and the BE conclusion |
| `dose_escalation` | `escalation` | The cohorts in order, the true and selected MTD, DLTs by dose, and the design's operating characteristics over 1,000 simulated trials |
| `pediatric_growth` | `height_velocity` | Annualized height velocity and change in height SDS by arm, and the non-inferiority analysis |
| `respiratory_exacerbation` | `exacerbations` | Exacerbation counts, exposure and rates by arm, the rate ratio, the dispersion, and FEV1 change |
| `vaccine` | `vaccine` | Geometric mean titers and seroconversion by arm, the GMT ratio, and reactogenicity by vaccination |
| `ophthalmology` | `bcva` | Mean change in BCVA and the proportion gaining 15 letters by arm, and the non-inferiority analysis |

Each section carries its own targets next to the realized values. A dose-escalation study, for
example, records the true DLT rate of every dose next to the DLTs it observed:

```{python}
esc = tf.study("dose_escalation", seed=1, method="3+3").truth["escalation"]
{k: esc[k] for k in ("method", "target", "true_mtd", "selected_mtd")}
```

The true MTD is the dose whose DLT rate is closest to the target rate. This 3+3 study selected the
dose above it, as small escalation studies often do; `operating_characteristics` reports how often
the same design, repeated 1,000 times, selects each dose.

## Calibrated targets

Where a control is a clinical target, trialforge solves for the latent model parameters that give
it. In the oncology archetypes, overall survival and progression follow Weibull proportional
hazards models linked by a Gaussian copula, and tumor courses follow RECIST 1.1. The medians and
hazard ratios have exact solutions; confirmed response rates (which depend on the assessment
schedule and the confirmation rule) are calibrated by simulation on a fixed 40,000-subject cohort.

```{python}
onc = tf.study("oncology_solid_tumor", n=400, seed=1, os_hr=0.7, orr=[0.4, 0.2])
onc.truth["targets"]
```

The realized values are what a standard analysis of this study's ADaM gives: Kaplan-Meier medians
and a stratified Cox hazard ratio with its 95% confidence interval.

```{python}
onc.truth["overall_survival"]
```

```{python}
onc.truth["confirmed_orr"]
```

### Latent and observed medians

A target describes the latent course, and an observed value depends on how the study looks at it.
Death is observed on the day it happens, so the realized overall survival median estimates the
target directly. Progression is different: it is only seen at a tumor assessment, every 8 weeks
here, so a progression is dated at the first assessment after it happens. The Kaplan-Meier curve of
progression-free survival steps down on the assessment dates, and its median falls on one of them:

```{python}
onc.truth["progression_free_survival"]["by_arm"]
```

The control arm's median is 5.5 months (the week 24 assessment, day 168), not the 4.5-month median
of the latent time to progression. Real studies have the same bias, which is why their medians
cluster on assessment dates. The hazard ratio is far less affected, since both arms are assessed on
the same schedule.

### Calibration

`truth["calibration"]` reports the response rates the calibrated model gives on the calibration
cohort, and whether every target was reachable. A rate above what the assessment schedule allows
(when too many subjects progress or die before a response can be confirmed, say) is clamped to the
highest reachable one:

```{python}
onc.truth["calibration"]
```

Calibration depends only on the controls, not on `n` or the seed, and its result is cached, so the
first study with a new set of oncology controls takes a moment longer than the next.

## Crossover on progression

With `crossover_prob`, control subjects who progress may switch to Drug A, and the manifest's
`crossover` section reports how many did:

```{python}
switch = tf.study("oncology_solid_tumor", n=400, seed=1, crossover_prob=0.5)
switch.truth["crossover"]
```

Compare the overall survival hazard ratio with the same study without crossover. Crossover happens
after progression, so progression-free survival is the same in both, but switching to Drug A lengthens
the control arm's survival and pulls the hazard ratio toward 1:

```{python}
no_switch = tf.study("oncology_solid_tumor", n=400, seed=1)
{
    "without": no_switch.truth["overall_survival"]["stratified_cox_hr"]["hr"],
    "with": switch.truth["overall_survival"]["stratified_cox_hr"]["hr"],
}
```

The target `os_hr` is still the effect without crossover; the realized one is what an
intention-to-treat analysis sees.

## Interim cuts

An interim cut of an event-driven study reports its cutoff date and how many subjects had been
randomized by then:

```{python}
tf.study("oncology_solid_tumor", n=400, seed=1, interim_months=12).truth["interim"]
```

Every realized value in an interim manifest comes from the interim data: fewer subjects, shorter
follow-up and fewer events. The targets are those of the full study.

## In files

`Study.write()` and `Study.write_submission()` write the manifest as `truth.json` next to the
datasets, so the answer key travels with the data. Read it back with `json.load()`; its keys and
values are the same as `Study.truth`.
